actions.justification: Patient has cold extremities, altered mental status, hypotension (MAP 54), and tachycardia — hallmarks of poor end-organ perfusion in cardiogenic shock. Perfusion assessment is the first step to characterize severity and guide vasopressor/inotrope decisions.
Volume status assessment is critical in cardiogenic shock to differentiate wet vs. dry profiles (cold-wet vs. cold-dry) which determines whether diuretics, fluid, or pure inotropic support is needed.

Echocardiography is the cornerstone diagnostic tool in cardiogenic shock — identifies reduced EF, wall motion abnormalities, valvular pathology, pericardial effusion/tamponade, and guides targeted therapy. Essential at time of presentation.

Patient is in cardiogenic shock with MAP 54, BP 72/45, SpO2 82%, and cold extremities. Inotropic support (e.g., dobutamine) is indicated to improve cardiac output and end-organ perfusion. Vasopressors/inotropes are first-line in cardiogenic shock when MAP is critically low.
Troponin is essential to evaluate for acute myocardial infarction as the underlying cause of cardiogenic shock. This is a critical diagnostic step per AHA heart failure/cardiogenic shock guidelines.

Urgent cardiology consultation is indicated for cardiogenic shock management, including evaluation for mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella), coronary angiography if ACS is suspected, and advanced hemodynamic monitoring.
BNP helps confirm heart failure etiology and severity in cardiogenic shock, guides ongoing management and prognostication.
BMP is essential in cardiogenic shock to assess renal function, electrolytes (K+, Na+), glucose, and BUN/creatinine — critical for safe inotrope and diuretic dosing decisions.
Chest X-ray will assess for pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, and alternative etiologies of acute dyspnea/hypoxia in this cardiogenic shock presentation.

Patient has SpO2 of 82% with cardiogenic shock, likely due to severe pulmonary edema. Inotrope is already started. A cautious dose of IV diuretic (e.g., furosemide) can reduce pulmonary congestion and improve oxygenation. While MAP is low (54), the primary driver of hypoxia appears to be volume overload/pulmonary edema. Vasodilator is avoided given profound hypotension (BP 72/45).

In cardiogenic shock with severely reduced MAP (54 mmHg), after inotrope initiation, cautious vasodilator therapy may reduce afterload and improve cardiac output. However, given MAP of 54 mmHg which is borderline, this must be used with extreme caution. This is the only available action and aligns with AHA heart failure guidelines for afterload reduction in cardiogenic shock once perfusion pressure is partially supported by inotropes.
Mandatory action - obtain focused history to identify precipitating cause of cardiogenic shock (prior HF, MI, medications, etc.)
Mandatory action - detailed physical exam to assess JVP, S3 gallop, peripheral edema, lung crackles, and perfusion status in cardiogenic shock
Mandatory action - ECG is critical in cardiogenic shock to identify STEMI, arrhythmia, or other precipitant requiring urgent intervention; patient has HR 120 and severely depressed BP
Mandatory action - comprehensive metabolic assessment needed to evaluate renal function, electrolytes, and glucose in this cardiogenic shock patient with severely compromised perfusion.
Mandatory action - CBC needed to evaluate for anemia contributing to hypoxia and hemodynamic instability, and to assess for infection or hematologic abnormalities.

Patient is in cardiogenic shock with MAP 54, SpO2 82%, altered mental status, and RR 32 - immediate ICU admission is critical for continuous hemodynamic monitoring, ventilatory support, and vasopressor/inotrope management.
